paper.title: Evaluating Inference-Time Defenses Against Package Hallucination in LLM-Generated Code
paper.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used for code generation, yet they frequently hallucinate non-existent software packages, creating exploitable entry points into the software supply chain. We make four contributions to this problem. First, we show that prior evaluation methodologies systematically inflate hallucination rates by misclassifying standard-library modules as hallucinations in some languages. For Python, the overestimation reaches 9.4 percentage points. Second, we evaluate seven inference-time defenses for mitigating package hallucinations, including five guided decoding strategies (Greedy, Contrastive, DoLa, Nudging, and Active Layer-Contrastive Decoding), an iterative self-refinement approach (Self-Refine), and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based defense.. Across eight models spanning five families and four programming languages (Python, JavaScript, Ruby, Rust), RAG reduces the package hallucination rate (PHR) in 18 of 32 model--language configurations. Third, we introduce Package Utility (PU) to assess whether defenses preserve valid and task-relevant recommendations. Among strategies evaluated, Greedy decoding provides the strongest average mitigation--utility trade-off. Fourth, we stress-test all strategies under adversarial prompts seeded with fabricated package names and find that PHR surges by up to 45 percentage points relative to standard prompts, with Ruby consistently the most vulnerable language (80.9--95.2\%). Under adversarial conditions, RAG and Self-Refine outperform all decoding-only strategies, indicating that robust defense requires either external grounding or iterative self-verification when prompts are actively hostile. Our results recast package hallucination as both a measurement problem and a decoding-time control problem, and they demonstrate that the choice of defense must be matched to the threat model and recommendation utility.

english.instructions: Are the title and abstract primarily written in English?

criteria.yes: The paper's title and abstract are primarily in English.
criteria.no: The paper's title and abstract are primarily in another language.
criteria.unclear: The available text is insufficient to determine the language.

journalOrConference.instructions: Is the publication type explicitly identifiable from the title or abstract? Do not infer publication venue or Scopus indexing from arXiv alone.

criteria.yes: The text explicitly identifies this as a journal or conference paper.
criteria.no: The text explicitly identifies a non-article format, such as a thesis, opinion piece, research agenda, or implementation report.
criteria.unclear: Publication type is not stated; arXiv alone is not evidence for either answer.

evaluatesAiCoding.instructions: Is the main empirical object AI-assisted software development, code generated by AI, or software developers' use, validation, or perceptions of coding assistants? Count studies of developer discussions about coding tools. Mere mention of coding agents is insufficient. Studies confined to scientific/research programming by domain researchers are outside this software-development scope unless generated software artifacts themselves are evaluated. Package hallucinations in generated code are directly in scope. Distinguish these from studies limited to package-installation behavior. Treat assistant package installation, general code-LLM program-semantics prediction, and agent benchmark methodology as adjacent rather than clearly in scope.

criteria.yes: The main findings directly concern generated code/products or developers' coding practices, evaluations, or perceptions of AI coding tools.
criteria.no: The AI coding connection is incidental, or the main subject is unrelated to generated code and software-development practice.
criteria.unclear: The study is adjacent to AI coding, but the title and abstract do not establish a direct outcome about generated code or coding practice.

empirical.instructions: Does this paper report its own empirical study with measured code outcomes, experiments, field observations, developer data, surveys, interviews, or other systematic evidence? Merely testing a new proposed artifact can be empirical while its primary contribution is still that artifact; answer this question independently of contribution focus.

criteria.yes: The paper reports original observations, measurements, experiments, interviews, surveys, or systematic analysis.
criteria.no: The paper is a conceptual argument, opinion, research agenda, or review of others' studies without its own empirical analysis.
criteria.unclear: The title and abstract do not establish whether original empirical analysis was performed.

focus.instructions: Identify the primary claimed contribution, not whether any experiments exist. Include empirical studies comparing defenses or mitigation strategies for defects in AI-generated code when the primary contribution is evidence about their effectiveness, limitations, or trade-offs. Evaluating interventions does not by itself make a paper solution-focused. Introducing a supporting metric also does not imply exclusion. Package hallucinations in generated code are directly in scope; distinguish them from studies limited to an agent's package-installation behavior. A new dataset/corpus, coding agent, detector, remediation method, workflow, pipeline, or benchmark for agent tasks/instruction-following is a particular artifact: mark 'solution' when introducing it is the main goal, even if it is evaluated. The exception is a framework designed specifically to assess AI-generated code or its properties; mark that 'unclear' when the paper mainly introduces the framework and supplies only an initial evaluation. A substantial independent empirical assessment of generated code or developer perceptions can be 'evaluation' even if a prevention method is also proposed. Profiling existing coding-agent benchmarks or behavior, rather than introducing one benchmark, can be 'unclear'.

criteria.evaluation: The primary contribution is independent empirical evidence about AI coding, its generated products, or developer experiences; any intervention is secondary.
criteria.solution: The primary contribution is a new artifact, method, dataset, benchmark, pipeline, or workflow, even when experiments demonstrate it.
criteria.unclear: An evaluation framework, adjacent benchmark study, or mixed evaluation-and-solution paper requires closer reading to identify its primary contribution.

decision.instructions: Initial title-and-abstract screening for a multivocal literature review of AI-generated coding in software development. Apply these rules in order. (1) Exclude explicitly non-English work, theses/opinion/reviews/research agendas, and work without original empirical evidence. An unknown venue is not an exclusion; do not invent Scopus indexing. (2) Include direct empirical evaluation of AI-generated code/products or software developers' use, verification, and perceptions of coding assistants. Developer-community discussions of coding tools count; human well-being/copresence with an incidental coding-agent mention does not. Scientific programming by domain researchers is outside this software-development scope unless the generated software product itself is evaluated. (3) Exclude papers whose main contribution is a new dataset/corpus, tool, detector, remediation technique, coding-agent pipeline, workflow, or a new benchmark of agent task/instruction-following performance, even if the authors run experiments on it. (4) Use 'maybe' for genuinely adjacent subjects such as package installation by coding agents, code-LLM prediction of program semantics, profiling existing agent benchmarks, or a framework primarily proposed to assess AI-generated code with limited validation. (5) A mixed paper can be included if it reports a substantial independent empirical evaluation of generated code and only then proposes a secondary mitigation; otherwise use 'maybe' or 'exclude' according to the primary aim. Include empirical studies comparing defenses or mitigation strategies for defects in AI-generated code when the primary contribution is evidence about their effectiveness, limitations, or trade-offs. Evaluating interventions does not by itself make a paper solution-focused. Introducing a supporting metric also does not imply exclusion. Package hallucinations in generated code are directly in scope; distinguish them from studies limited to an agent's package-installation behavior. Choose 'include' only for a clear fit, 'maybe' for a real boundary case requiring full-text review, and 'exclude' for a clear violation. Do not default to 'maybe' merely because a proposed artifact includes experiments. Labels: include=Definitely include; maybe=Maybe include; exclude=Definitely exclude.
